# Exercise Solutions

These are the solutions to the exercises used in the course.

The solutions use these packages (others are loaded where they are needed):

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-setup, message = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Californian bird diversity

1. Import the data as an object called `birds`, then check the columns with `str()`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-1}
birds <- read.csv("CourseData/suburbanBirds.csv")
str(birds)
```

There are 17 suburbs and the five columns `Name`, `Year`, `HabitatIndex`, `nIndividuals` and `nSpecies`. (`HabitatIndex` has one missing value, `NA`.)

2. Calculate the mean, minimum, and maximum of `nSpecies`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-2}
mean(birds$nSpecies)
min(birds$nSpecies)
max(birds$nSpecies)
```

There is more than one way to do this. For example, `range(birds$nSpecies)` gives the minimum and maximum together, and `summary(birds$nSpecies)` gives all three (and more).

3. Create a new column with `birds$Age <- 1975 - birds$Year` and check that it looks sensible.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-3}
birds$Age <- 1975 - birds$Year
range(birds$Age)
```

The suburbs were between 1 and 29 years old when they were surveyed.

4. Plot `Age` against `nSpecies`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-4}
plot(birds$Age, birds$nSpecies)
```

5. Add a smoother.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-5}
plot(birds$Age, birds$nSpecies)
lines(lowess(birds$Age, birds$nSpecies))
```

Species richness increases with the age of the suburb: the newest suburbs have only 3 to 6 species, while those built 20 or more years before the survey have 11 to 15. The smoother suggests that richness rises steeply over the first 15 to 20 years and then levels off. A possible explanation is that the gardens, parks and trees that come with development take years to mature, and as they do they provide habitat for more species.


## Wrangling the Amniote Life History Database

1. When you have imported the data, use `dim` to check the dimensions of the whole data frame (you should see that there are `r ncol(amniote)` columns and `r nrow(amniote)` rows). Use `names` to look at the names of all columns in the data in `amniote`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-6}
amniote <- read.csv("CourseData/Amniote_Database_Aug_2015.csv",
  na.strings = "-999"
)
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-7}
dim(amniote)
names(amniote)
```

2. We are interested in longevity (lifespan), body size and reproductive effort, and how this might vary depending on the taxonomy (specifically, with Class). Use `select` to pick relevant columns of the dataset and discard the others. Call the new data frame `x`. 
The relevant columns are the taxonomic variables (`class`, `genus` & `species`) and `longevity_y`, `litter_or_clutch_size_n`, `litters_or_clutches_per_y`, and `adult_body_mass_g`.


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-8}
x <- amniote %>%
  select(
    class, genus, species,
    longevity_y, adult_body_mass_g,
    litter_or_clutch_size_n, litters_or_clutches_per_y
  )
```

3. Take a look at the first few entries in the `species` column. You will see that it is only the *epithet*, the second part of the *Genus_species* name, that is given.  
Use `mutate` and `paste` to convert the `species` column to a *Genus_species* by pasting the data in `genus` and `species` together. To see how this works, try out the following command, `paste(1:3, 4:6)`. After you have created the new column, remove the `genus` column (using `select` and `-genus`).


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-9}
x <- x %>%
  mutate(species = paste(genus, species)) %>%
  select(-genus)
head(x)
```

4. What is the longest living species in the record? Use `arrange` to sort the data from longest to shortest longevity (`longevity_y`), and then look at the top of the file using `head` to find out. (hint: you will need to use reverse sort (`-`)). Cut and paste the species name into Google to find out more!

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-10}
x <- x %>% arrange(-longevity_y)
head(x)
```

5. Do the same thing but this time find the shortest lived species. Is this result plausible? What might have gone wrong?

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-11}
x <- x %>% arrange(longevity_y)
head(x)
```

The two shortest-lived species, the northern marsupial mole (*Notoryctes caurinus*) and the Indian hare (*Lepus nigricollis*), are recorded as living 1 month (0.083 years). That is not plausible for mammals of this size (the hare weighs over 2 kg). These values are almost certainly errors in the database, for example a value in months entered as years, or a juvenile life stage recorded as the life span. Real data sets often contain errors like this, which is why it is worth checking extreme values before analysing them.

6. Use `summarise` and `group_by` to make a table summarising `min`, `median` and `max` life spans (`longevity_y`) for the three taxonomic classes in the database. Remember that you need to tell R to remove the `NA` values using a `na.rm = TRUE` argument.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-12}
x %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    min = min(longevity_y, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(longevity_y, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(longevity_y, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

7. Body size is thought to be associated with life span. Let's treat that as a hypothesis and test it graphically. Sketch what the graph would look like if the hypothesis were true, and if it was false. Plot `adult_body_mass_g` vs. `longevity_y` (using base R graphics). You should notice that this looks a bit messy.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-13}
plot(x$adult_body_mass_g, x$longevity_y)
```

8. Use `mutate` to create a new `log`-transformed variables, `logMass` and `logLongevity`. Use these to make a "log-log" plot. You should see that makes the relationship more linear, and easier to "read".

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-14}
x <- x %>%
  mutate(
    logMass = log(adult_body_mass_g),
    logLongevity = log(longevity_y)
  )

plot(x$logMass, x$logLongevity)
```

9. Is there a trade-off between reproductive effort and life span? Think about this as a hypothesis - sketch what the graph would look like if that were true, and if it was false. Now use the data to test that hypothesis: Use `mutate` to create a variable called `logOffspring` which is the logarithm of (number of litters/clutches per year × number of babies in each litter/clutch), i.e. `log(litters_or_clutches_per_y * litter_or_clutch_size_n)`. Then plot `logOffspring` vs. `logLongevity`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-15}
x <- x %>%
  mutate(logOffspring = log(
    litter_or_clutch_size_n * litters_or_clutches_per_y
  ))

plot(x$logOffspring, x$logLongevity)
```

10. To answer the final question (differences between taxonomic classes) you could now use `filter` to subset to particular classes and repeat the plot to see whether the relationship holds universally. 

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-16}
aves <- x %>%
  filter(class == "Aves")

plot(aves$logOffspring, aves$logLongevity)
title("Aves")
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-17}
mammalia <- x %>%
  filter(class == "Mammalia")

plot(mammalia$logOffspring, mammalia$logLongevity)
title("Mammalia")
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-18}
reptilia <- x %>%
  filter(class == "Reptilia")

plot(reptilia$logOffspring, reptilia$logLongevity)
title("Reptilia")
```

## Temperature effects on egg laying dates

1. Import the egg data and take a look at it with `head` or `str`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-19, eval=TRUE}
eggDates <- read.csv("CourseData/eggDates.csv")
head(eggDates)
```

2. Use `pivot_longer` to reformat the data, and make sure `Year` is numeric.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-20}
eggDates <- eggDates %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("y"),
    names_to = "Year", values_to = "dayNumber",
    names_prefix = "y"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.numeric(Year))

head(eggDates)
```

(Without `names_prefix`, you could instead remove the "y" afterwards with `mutate(Year = gsub(pattern = "y", replacement = "", Year))`.)

3. Calculate the mean egg date per year using `summarise`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-22}
meanEgg <- eggDates %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(meanEggDate = mean(dayNumber, na.rm = TRUE))

meanEgg
```

4. Import the weather data and take a look at it with `head` or `str`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-23,eval=TRUE}
weather <- read.csv("CourseData/AarslevTemperature.csv")
str(weather)
```

5. Use `filter` to subset to the months of interest (February to April) and then `summarise` the data to calculate the mean temperature in this period.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-24}
weather <- weather %>%
  filter(MONTH %in% 2:4) %>%
  group_by(YEAR) %>%
  summarise(meanSpringTemp = mean(TEMP))

head(weather)
```

6. Join the two yearly datasets together using `left_join`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-25}
joinedData <- left_join(meanEgg, weather, by = c("Year" = "YEAR"))
joinedData
```

7. Plot a graph of `meanSpringTemp` on the x-axis and `meanEggDate` on the y-axis.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-26}
plot(joinedData$meanSpringTemp, joinedData$meanEggDate,
  xlab = "Mean February-April temperature (°C)",
  ylab = "Mean first egg date (day of year)"
)
```

Is laying date associated with spring temperature? There looks to be a negative relationship: in warmer springs, the birds start laying earlier. But we should not be too confident. There are only six years of data, and much of the pattern comes from one year: 2013 had a very cold spring and the latest mean laying date. With more years we could test the relationship properly (you will learn how to do this with linear regression later in the course).

## Virtual dice

Let's try the same kind of thing with the roll of (virtual) dice.

Here's how to do one roll of the dice:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-27, echo=-1, results='asis',cache = TRUE}
set.seed(123)
diceRoll <- 1:6
sample(diceRoll, 1)
```

1) Simulate 10 rolls of the dice, and make a table of results.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-28, echo=-1,cache = TRUE}
set.seed(123)
result <- sample(diceRoll, 10, replace = TRUE)
table(result)
```

Your table will probably look different to this, because it is a random process. You may notice that some numbers in the table are missing if some numbers were never rolled by our virtual dice. 

2) Now simulate 90 rolls of the dice, and plot the results as a bar plot using `geom_bar` in `ggplot`. Add a horizontal line using `geom_hline` to show the **expected** result based on what you know about probability.


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-29, echo=-1,fig.cap=('Barplot of 90 simulated dice throws'),cache = TRUE}
set.seed(2)
n <- 90
result <- data.frame(result = sample(diceRoll, n, replace = TRUE))

ggplot(result, aes(x = result)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = n / 6)
```

3) Try adjusting the code to simulate dice rolls with small (say, 30) and large (say, 600, or 6000, or 9000) samples. Observe what happens to the proportions, and compare them to the expected value. What does this tell you about the importance of sample size when trying to estimate real phenomena?


You only need to edit the `n <- 90` line in the code above

The main message here is that as sample size increases you are more likely to obtain a good estimate of the true value of the phenomenon.  You may also notice that,  what would be considered a good sample size for the coin flipping (i.e. it recovers the true probability of 0.5 reasonably well) is NOT adequate for getting a good estimate of the probabilities for the dice.

This is because of the different number of possibilities: as the range of possible outcomes increases, the sample size requirements increase. In other words, choosing a good sample size is context-dependent.


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-30, echo= FALSE,fig.cap=('Barplots of 30 and 9000 simulated dice throws'),cache = TRUE}
set.seed(2)
n <- 30
result <- data.frame(result = sample(diceRoll, n, replace = TRUE))

A <- ggplot(result, aes(x = result)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = n / 6) +
  ggtitle("n = 30")

set.seed(2)
n <- 9000 # Vary this number
result <- data.frame(result = sample(diceRoll, n, replace = TRUE))

B <- ggplot(result, aes(x = result)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = n / 6) +
  ggtitle("n = 9000")

A + B
```


## Sexual selection in Hercules beetles

**Task 1: Explore the data.**

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-31}
hercules <- read.csv("CourseData/herculesBeetle.csv")
str(hercules)

# Set the factor levels so that diff() gives Male minus Female
hercules$sex <- factor(hercules$sex, levels = c("Female", "Male"))
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-32, echo = -1}
set.seed(42)
ggplot(hercules, aes(x = sex, y = width)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Width (cm)")
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-33}
meanVals <- hercules %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(width), sd = sd(width), .groups = "drop")
meanVals
```

Males are wider on average (about `r round(meanVals$mean[2], 1)` cm) than females (about `r round(meanVals$mean[1], 1)` cm), but the two groups overlap a lot.

**Task 2: Formulate hypotheses.**

*Null hypothesis:* sex is unrelated to width, so the sex labels are exchangeable.

*Alternative hypothesis:* males are wider than females. The research idea (sexual selection on males) predicts a direction before we look at the data, so a **one-sided** test is appropriate. (If we had no prior expectation of which sex is larger, we would use a two-sided test.)

**Task 3: Calculate the observed statistic.** The statistic is the mean width of males minus the mean width of females, so positive values support the alternative.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-35}
observedDiff <- hercules %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(width), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pull(mean) %>%
  diff()
observedDiff
```

**Task 4: Construct a null distribution.** We shuffle the sex labels, keeping 10 males and 10 females. Under the null hypothesis, sex is unrelated to width, so any allocation of the labels to the 20 measurements is equally plausible.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-37, echo = -1}
set.seed(43)
# Check the code with a few randomisations first
replicate(
  5,
  hercules %>%
    mutate(sex = sample(sex)) %>%
    group_by(sex) %>%
    summarise(mean = mean(width), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pull(mean) %>%
    diff()
)
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-38, echo = -1}
set.seed(44)
B <- 10000

diffs <- data.frame(
  diffs = replicate(
    B,
    hercules %>%
      mutate(sex = sample(sex)) %>%
      group_by(sex) %>%
      summarise(mean = mean(width), .groups = "drop") %>%
      pull(mean) %>%
      diff()
  )
)
```

**Task 5: Evaluate the evidence.**

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-39, message = FALSE}
ggplot(diffs, aes(x = diffs)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observedDiff, colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Difference between means (Male - Female, cm)",
    y = "Number of randomised datasets"
  )
```

Because the alternative predicts a positive difference, we count randomised differences greater than or equal to the observed one, and use the +1 correction:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-40}
b <- sum(diffs$diffs >= observedDiff)
p_value <- (b + 1) / (B + 1)
b
p_value
```

For comparison, the exact one-sided p-value from all 184,756 possible allocations of 10 males and 10 females is 2,202/184,756 = 0.012, very close to the Monte Carlo estimate.

**Task 6: Write a short results paragraph.**

*"Mean width was `r round(meanVals$mean[2], 2)` cm in males and `r round(meanVals$mean[1], 2)` cm in females (n = 10 per sex), a difference of `r round(observedDiff, 2)` cm (Male minus Female). A one-sided Monte Carlo randomisation test, in which the sex labels were randomly reallocated 10,000 times while preserving group sizes, provided evidence that males are wider than females (p = `r round(p_value, 3)`). This is consistent with sexual selection on male size, although these data alone cannot show that sexual selection is the cause."*

**Is the difference biologically important?** A statistically clear difference is not automatically an important one. Here the difference (about 2.3 cm, or about 16% of mean female width) is fairly large relative to body size. To judge its importance we would want to know, for example, whether wider males win more fights or mate more often, how the difference compares with variation among populations, and whether width is a good measure of overall body size.

## Sex differences in fine motor skills

Some people have suggested that there might be sex differences in fine motor skills in humans. Use the data collected from students in previous years to address this topic using t-tests. The relevant data set is called `classData.csv`, and the columns of interest are `Gender` and `Precision`.

Carry out a two-sample t-test. 

1) Plot the data (e.g. with a box plot, or histogram)

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-41,echo = -1,cache=TRUE}
set.seed(12)
classData <- read.csv("CourseData/classData.csv") %>%
  filter(Gender %in% c("Male", "Female")) %>% 
  filter(Year == 2019) #you may use a different filter

ggplot(classData, aes(x = Gender, y = Precision)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2)
```


2) Formulate null and alternative hypotheses. 

*Null hypothesis:* the mean precision score is the same for males and females.

*Alternative hypothesis:* the mean precision score differs between males and females (a two-sided alternative, because we have no strong reason to expect a particular direction).

3) Use the `t.test` function to do the test.


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-42}
t.test(Precision ~ Gender, data = classData)
```

4) Write a sentence or two describing the results.
```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-43, echo = FALSE}
x <- t.test(Precision ~ Gender, data = classData)
```
There was no clear difference in mean precision between females and males (Welch's t-test: t = `r format(x$statistic,nsmall = 2,digits = 3)`, df = `r format(x$parameter,nsmall = 2,digits = 3)`, p = `r format(x$p.value,nsmall = 2,digits = 3)`). The 95% confidence interval for the difference (female minus male) was `r sprintf(x$conf.int[1], fmt = '%#.3f')` to `r sprintf(x$conf.int[2], fmt = '%#.3f')`, which includes zero. We therefore have no evidence of a difference, but this is not the same as showing that there is no difference: the interval shows which differences are still compatible with the data. (These are also observational data from a convenience sample, so we should be careful about generalising.)

## Therapy for anorexia

A study was carried out looking at the effect of cognitive behavioural therapy on weight of people with anorexia. Weight was measured in week 1 and again in week 8. Use a paired t-test to assess whether weight changed between week 1 and week 8 during the treatment. (Think about this: the study has no control group, so can a change in weight on its own tell you that the *treatment* caused it?)

The data is called `anorexiaCBT.csv`

The data are in "wide format". You may wish to convert it to "long format" depending on how you use the data. You can do that with the `pivot_longer` function, which rearranges the data:


1) Plot the data (e.g. with an interaction plot).

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-44,echo=TRUE,message=FALSE}
anorexiaCBT <- read.csv("CourseData/anorexiaCBT.csv",
  header = TRUE
)

anorexiaCBT_long <- anorexiaCBT %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Week"), names_to = "time",
    values_to = "weight"
  )
```

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-45}
ggplot(anorexiaCBT_long, aes(
  x = time, y = weight,
  group = Subject
)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("Time") +
  ylab("Weight (lb)")
```



2) Formulate a null and alternative hypothesis.

*Null hypothesis:* the mean change in weight between week 1 and week 8 is zero.

*Alternative hypothesis:* the mean change in weight is not zero (two-sided). You could argue for a one-sided alternative (weight *increases*), but only if that was decided before looking at the data.

3) Use `t.test` to conduct a *paired* t-test.

Putting week 8 first means the estimate is week 8 minus week 1, so a weight gain is positive:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-46}
t.test(anorexiaCBT$Week08, anorexiaCBT$Week01, paired = TRUE)
```


4) Write a couple of sentences to report your result.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-48}
x <- t.test(anorexiaCBT$Week08, anorexiaCBT$Week01, paired = TRUE)
```

On average, weight increased by `r sprintf(x$estimate, fmt= '%#.1f')` lb (about `r sprintf(0.4536 * x$estimate, fmt= '%#.1f')` kg) between week 1 and week 8 (paired t-test: t = `r format(x$statistic,nsmall = 2,digits = 3)`, df = `r format(x$parameter,nsmall = 2,digits = 3)`, p = `r format(x$p.value,nsmall = 2,digits = 3)`; 95% CI for the mean change `r sprintf(x$conf.int[1], fmt = '%#.1f')` to `r sprintf(x$conf.int[2], fmt = '%#.1f')` lb). This is evidence that weight changed during the treatment period. However, because there is no control group, it does not show that CBT *caused* the change: weight might have changed anyway over those weeks (for example because of other care the patients received, or because people tend to enter treatment when their weight is at its lowest).

## Compare t-tests with randomisation tests

```{block 6-1-00-AllSolutions-49, type="do-something"}
Try re-fitting some of these tests as randomisation tests (or analyse the randomisation test data using `t.test`). Do they give approximately the same results? 

Then try answering the question - "*are people who prefer dogs taller than those who prefer cats?* " using the `classData.csv`. Can you think of any problems with this analysis?
```

The problem with the analysis is that it is likely to be *confounded* by gender. Men are on average taller than women. If men and women also differ in whether they prefer cats or dogs, then a height difference between "cat people" and "dog people" could simply reflect the different proportions of men and women in the two groups, rather than anything to do with pet preference.

## Apple tree crop yield

Import the data (`apples.csv`) and analyse it using the techniques you have learned in the ANOVA lecture, and the previous worksheet, to answer the question "What is the effect of tree spacing on apple yields?"

1. Import and look at the data (e.g. `summary` or `str` or `head`)

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-50}
apples <- read.csv("CourseData/apples.csv")
summary(apples)
```

2. Ensure that the explanatory variable (`spacing`) is defined as a categorical variable (i.e. a "factor", in R-speak). You can use `mutate` and `as.factor` functions for this.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-51}
apples <- apples %>%
  mutate(spacing = as.factor(spacing))
```



3. Plot the data using `ggplot` (a box plot with (optionally) added jittered points would be good).

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-52, echo = -1,cache=TRUE}
set.seed(42)
ggplot(apples, aes(x = spacing, y = yield)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  xlab("Spacing (feet)") +
  ylab("Yield (kg per tree)")
```

4. Fit an ANOVA model using `lm`. 


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-53}
apple_mod <- lm(yield ~ spacing, data = apples)
```

5. Check the model using a diagnostic plot (i.e. using `autoplot` from the `ggfortify` package).

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-54,message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ggfortify)
autoplot(apple_mod)
```

Look for points in the Q-Q plot lying close to the line (normality) and for the three columns of residuals in the Residuals vs Fitted and Scale-Location plots having a broadly similar spread (equal variance).


6. Use `anova` to get the ANOVA summary.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-55}
anova(apple_mod)
```

7. You should see that there are differences among treatments. But where are those differences? Use `summary` on  your model to find out.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-56}
summary(apple_mod)
```

8. Use a Tukey test to make all the pairwise comparisons among the treatments.

`TukeyHSD` gives the estimated differences with 95% confidence intervals (adjusted for multiple comparisons). Note that `aov` (like `lm`) drops the rows with missing yields:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-57}
apple_tukey <- TukeyHSD(aov(yield ~ spacing, data = apples))
apple_tukey
```

The letters version from `agricolae` gives the same conclusions:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-57b}
library(agricolae)
HSD.test(apple_mod, "spacing", console = TRUE)
```


9. Write a few sentences that summarise your findings. What biological processes do you think drive the effects that you have detected?

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-58,echo = FALSE}
x <- anova(apple_mod)
appleMeans <- apples %>%
  group_by(spacing) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(yield, na.rm = TRUE))
fmt <- function(v) formatC(v, digits = 1, format = "f")
tk <- apple_tukey$spacing
```

*Mean yield per tree differed among the three spacings (ANOVA: F = `r formatC(x$"F value"[1], digits = 2, format = "f")`, d.f. = `r x$Df[1]` and `r x$Df[2]`, p = `r formatC(x$"Pr(>F)"[1], digits = 4, format = "f")`; see the box plot above). Trees planted 6 feet apart yielded the least (mean `r fmt(appleMeans$mean[1])` kg per tree), compared with `r fmt(appleMeans$mean[2])` kg at 10 feet and `r fmt(appleMeans$mean[3])` kg at 14 feet. Compared with the 6-foot spacing, yield per tree was `r fmt(tk["10-6", "diff"])` kg higher at 10 feet (95% CI `r fmt(tk["10-6", "lwr"])` to `r fmt(tk["10-6", "upr"])`; Tukey HSD) and `r fmt(tk["14-6", "diff"])` kg higher at 14 feet (95% CI `r fmt(tk["14-6", "lwr"])` to `r fmt(tk["14-6", "upr"])`). The difference between 10 and 14 feet was smaller and not clear (`r fmt(tk["14-10", "diff"])` kg, 95% CI `r fmt(tk["14-10", "lwr"])` to `r fmt(tk["14-10", "upr"])`).*

**What biological processes might drive this?** Trees that are closer together compete more strongly for light, water and nutrients, so each tree has fewer resources to put into growth and fruit. Shading of the lower canopy by neighbouring trees may be particularly important for fruit production. Beyond about 10 feet, the extra space seems to make less difference, perhaps because competition between neighbours is already weak.

Note that these are yields **per tree**. A grower is usually more interested in yield **per hectare**: closely spaced trees produce less each, but there are many more of them, so the total yield per hectare could still be higher at the 6-foot spacing. Which spacing is "best" therefore depends on the question you ask.

10. Optional. Instead of using a Tukey test, use the alternative "relevel" approach to make the missing comparison.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-59}
apples2 <- apples %>%
  mutate(spacing = relevel(spacing, ref = "10"))
apple_mod2 <- lm(yield ~ spacing, data = apples2)
summary(apple_mod2)
```


-------
If you get this far, try using the ANOVA approach on one of the previous two-sample t-test examples (remember that ANOVA can be used when your single explanatory variable has TWO or more levels). You should notice that the results are the same whether you use the `t.test` function with `var.equal = TRUE` or the ANOVA approach with `lm` (for two groups, F = t^2^). The default Welch t-test gives slightly different results, because it does not assume equal variances.

## Is foot length worth adding?

1. Import the data and convert the measurements to cm.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-foot-1}
morph <- read.csv("CourseData/morphometry.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    Height = Height / 10,
    HandLength = HandLength / 10,
    FootLength = FootLength / 10
  ) # mm -> cm
```

2. Reproduce the model from the chapter.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-foot-2, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ggfortify)
mod_int <- lm(Height ~ HandLength * Sex, data = morph)
autoplot(mod_int)
anova(mod_int)
mod_B <- lm(Height ~ HandLength + Sex, data = morph)
summary(mod_B)
```

The diagnostic plots look acceptable. The interaction is not needed (F = 0.17, d.f. = 1 and 151, p = 0.68), so we use the parallel-lines model `mod_B`: height increases by 3.9 cm per cm of hand length (SE 0.40), and males are 7.4 cm taller than females with the same hand length.

3. Foot length against hand length.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-foot-3}
ggplot(morph, aes(x = HandLength, y = FootLength, colour = Sex)) +
  geom_point()
cor(morph$HandLength, morph$FootLength)
```

The two are strongly correlated (r = 0.90): people with long hands nearly always have long feet. (The correlation is still high within each sex: 0.75 in males and 0.80 in females.) So the data contain little information about the effect of one with the other held constant, and we should expect at least one of the estimates to become uncertain.

4. Foot length without hand length.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-foot-4}
mod_F <- lm(Height ~ FootLength + Sex, data = morph)
summary(mod_F)
confint(mod_F)
```

On its own (with sex), foot length predicts height well: 1.75 cm of height per cm of foot length (95% CI 1.18 to 2.31, p < 0.001). Adjusted $R^2$ = 0.74, a little lower than the hand-length model (0.80).

5. Both length measurements in the same model.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-foot-5}
mod_HF <- lm(Height ~ HandLength + FootLength + Sex, data = morph)
summary(mod_HF)
confint(mod_HF)
anova(mod_B, mod_HF)
```

* Foot length: the estimate drops from 1.75 to -0.37 cm per cm (SE 0.39, p = 0.34; 95% CI -1.15 to 0.40). Once hand length is in the model, foot length adds nothing detectable (comparing `mod_B` and `mod_HF`: F = 0.91, d.f. = 1 and 151, p = 0.34).
* Hand length: the standard error rises from 0.40 to 0.62, so the estimate becomes less precise, even though nothing about hand length has changed.
* Adjusted $R^2$: 0.803 in both `mod_B` and `mod_HF`. Adding foot length explains no extra variation.

6. Summing up.

Hand length and foot length are so strongly correlated (r = 0.90) that the model cannot separate their effects: with both in the model, foot length's estimate collapses towards zero and the hand-length estimate becomes less precise. This is called multicollinearity. It is not an error in R, and it does not mean that foot length is unrelated to height (on its own it predicts height well). I would report `mod_B` (`Height ~ HandLength + Sex`), because it fits as well as the model with both measurements and its estimates are more precise. The general lesson: check correlations between explanatory variables (with `cor()` or a plot) before fitting, and when two are almost the same, choose one (or combine them) rather than fitting both.


## Fish behaviour

1. Import the data set, `fishPersonality.csv`

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-68}
fishPersonality <- read.csv("CourseData/fishPersonality.csv")
```

2. Plot the data (e.g. as a box plot)

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-69}
ggplot(fishPersonality, aes(
  x = colouration, y = spawning,
  fill = personality
)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

3. Fit an ANOVA model using `lm`.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-70}
mod_A <- lm(spawning ~ personality + colouration +
  personality:colouration, data = fishPersonality)
```

4. Look at diagnostic plots from this model (`autoplot`)

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-fish-diag, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ggfortify)
autoplot(mod_A)
```

The diagnostic plots look acceptable: no strong pattern in the residuals and no extreme points.

5. Use `anova` to get an Analysis of Variance summary table. Start with the interaction row.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-71}
anova(mod_A)
```

The interaction is not significant (F = 2.91, d.f. = 1 and 28, p = 0.099), so there is no clear evidence that the effect of personality depends on colour pattern. This is **not** the same as showing that there is no interaction. The group means in the plot are clearly not parallel (proactive fish spawn about 54 more eggs than reactive fish in heterogeneous fish, but only about 9 more in homogeneous fish), and with only 8 fish per group the test has little power to detect an interaction of this size. The honest conclusion is "no clear evidence", and a larger study would be needed to settle it.

6. The interaction is not needed, so drop it and refit the model with the main effects only.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-72}
mod_B <- lm(spawning ~ personality + colouration, data = fishPersonality)
anova(mod_B)
```

Both main effects are significant: personality (F = 5.16, d.f. = 1 and 29, p = 0.031) and colouration (F = 37.1, d.f. = 1 and 29, p < 0.001). Colouration explains much more of the variation than personality (sum of squares 55862 vs 7781).

7. Get the coefficient summary and confidence intervals of the final model, and interpret them.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-73}
summary(mod_B)
confint(mod_B)
```

* The intercept (207.2) is the estimated spawning of the reference group: proactive, heterogeneous fish.
* `personalityReactive` (-31.2, 95% CI -59.3 to -3.1): reactive fish spawn about 31 fewer eggs than proactive fish of the same colour morph.
* `colourationHomogeneous` (83.6, 95% CI 55.5 to 111.6): homogeneous fish spawn about 84 more eggs than heterogeneous fish of the same personality.
* Each variable has only two levels, so these coefficients already compare the two groups and no post-hoc test is needed.

8. Sum up your findings with reference to the initial research questions.

* Both colour pattern and personality are associated with spawning. Colour pattern has the larger effect: homogeneous fish spawned about 84 more eggs than heterogeneous fish (95% CI 55 to 112; F = 37.1, d.f. = 1 and 29, p < 0.001), while proactive fish spawned about 31 more than reactive fish (95% CI 3 to 59; F = 5.16, d.f. = 1 and 29, p = 0.031).
* There was no clear evidence that the effect of personality depends on colour pattern (interaction F = 2.91, d.f. = 1 and 28, p = 0.099). The plot hints that the personality difference may be larger in heterogeneous fish, but with 8 fish per group this study cannot tell; it would need a larger sample.
* Do not conclude that "personality matters only in heterogeneous fish" from separate comparisons within each colour morph (e.g. Tukey tests on the four groups). A significant difference in one group and a non-significant one in the other does not show that the two differences are themselves different: that is exactly what the interaction test assesses.


## Maze runner


1. Import the data and graph it (`geom_boxplot`). Try adding the points to the `ggplot` using the new (to you) function `geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")`.


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-74}
maze <- read.csv("CourseData/maze.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
head(maze)

(A <- ggplot(maze, aes(x = Age, y = nErrors)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center"))
```

2. Fit an appropriate GLM.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-75}
mod_A <- glm(nErrors ~ Age, data = maze, family = poisson)
```

3. Examine the diagnostic plots of the model (`autoplot`).

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-76,message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ggfortify)
autoplot(mod_A)
```

4. Get the analysis of variance (deviance) table (`anova`). What does this tell you?

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-77}
anova(mod_A, test = "Chi")
```


5. Obtain the `summary` table. What does this tell you?

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-78}
summary(mod_A)
```

6. Use the model to get the predicted average number of mistakes for each age group (plus/minus 95% confidence interval). Start from a data frame of the groups to predict for, `newData <- data.frame(Age = c("Adult", "Child"))`. Remember that (i) the model summary is on the scale of the linear predictor, so `exp(AgeChild)` is the *ratio* of the Child mean to the Adult mean, not the Child mean itself; and (ii) the standard error of the Child mean is not in the `summary` table (it combines both coefficients), so use `predict(..., se.fit = TRUE)` as in the fox example: calculate the 95% CI as the fit plus/minus 1.96 times the standard error on the link scale, then back-transform. Ask for help if you get stuck.

The `AgeChild` coefficient, back-transformed, is the ratio of the Child mean to the Adult mean: children make about three times as many mistakes. (`confint()` gives a profile-likelihood interval, which can differ slightly from estimate plus/minus 1.96 SE.)

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-79a}
exp(coef(mod_A))
exp(confint(mod_A))
```

The group means and their 95% confidence intervals come from `predict()`:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-79}
newData <- data.frame(Age = c("Child", "Adult"))
pv <- predict(mod_A, newData, se.fit = TRUE)

newData <- newData %>%
  mutate(nErrors_LP = pv$fit) %>%
  mutate(lowerCI_LP = pv$fit - 1.96 * pv$se.fit) %>%
  mutate(upperCI_LP = pv$fit + 1.96 * pv$se.fit)

inverseFunction <- family(mod_A)$linkinv

newData <- newData %>%
  mutate(nErrors = inverseFunction(nErrors_LP)) %>%
  mutate(lowerCI = inverseFunction(lowerCI_LP)) %>%
  mutate(upperCI = inverseFunction(upperCI_LP))


A + geom_point(
  data = newData, aes(x = Age, y = nErrors),
  colour = "red"
) +
  geom_segment(data = newData, aes(
    x = Age, xend = Age,
    y = lowerCI, yend = upperCI
  ), colour = "red")
```


## Forensic footprints

1. Import the reference data and create a binary (0/1) response for the probability of being male.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-82}
morph <- read.csv("CourseData/morphometry.csv") %>%
  mutate(male = ifelse(Sex == "Male", 1, 0))
head(morph)
```

2. Plot the data.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-83, echo=-1,fig.width=5,fig.height=3,fig.align='center',message=FALSE}
set.seed(42)
(A <- ggplot(morph, aes(x = FootLength, y = male)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5))
```

3. Fit the binomial GLM - this is our "forensic tool".

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-84}
morphMod <- glm(male ~ FootLength, data = morph, family = binomial)
```

4. Check the model using `DHARMa`. The points fall on the QQ diagonal and the residual-versus-predicted plot is a random star-field with no patterns, so the binomial family is appropriate.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-85,fig.width=6,fig.height=4,fig.align='center',message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
library(DHARMa)
sim_res <- simulateResiduals(fittedModel = morphMod)
plot(sim_res)
```

5. The analysis of deviance table and coefficient summary. Foot length is a highly significant predictor of sex, and the positive slope shows that the probability of being male increases with foot length.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-86}
anova(morphMod, test = "Chi")
summary(morphMod)
```

6. How good is the forensic tool? Predict the probability of being male for everyone in the reference data, classify as male when that probability exceeds 0.5, and compare with the truth. The confusion table and the overall accuracy show that the tool classifies about 90% of people correctly - good, but far from perfect because male and female foot lengths overlap.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-87}
morph <- morph %>%
  mutate(pMale = predict(morphMod, type = "response")) %>%
  mutate(prediction = ifelse(pMale > 0.5, "Male", "Female"))

# Confusion table: true sex versus predicted sex
table(trueSex = morph$Sex, prediction = morph$prediction)

# Overall proportion correctly classified
mean(morph$prediction == morph$Sex)
```

7. The crime scene. Predict the probability that the person with a 271 mm foot was male, with a 95% confidence interval, back-transforming to the probability scale with the inverse link function.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-88}
crimeScene <- data.frame(FootLength = 271)

pv <- predict(morphMod, newdata = crimeScene, se.fit = TRUE)
inverseFunction <- family(morphMod)$linkinv

crimeScene <- crimeScene %>%
  mutate(
    probMale = inverseFunction(pv$fit),
    lowerCI = inverseFunction(pv$fit - 1.96 * pv$se.fit),
    upperCI = inverseFunction(pv$fit + 1.96 * pv$se.fit)
  )
crimeScene
```

The probability of being male is very high (well above 0.9), so the evidence points strongly to a male culprit. Note, however, that "very likely" is not "certain": one woman in the reference data has a foot this large, so on its own this would be suggestive rather than conclusive evidence.

8. The second print (249 mm). Repeat the prediction for a foot length of 249 mm.

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-89}
crimeScene2 <- data.frame(FootLength = 249)
pv2 <- predict(morphMod, newdata = crimeScene2, se.fit = TRUE)

crimeScene2 <- crimeScene2 %>%
  mutate(
    probMale = inverseFunction(pv2$fit),
    lowerCI = inverseFunction(pv2$fit - 1.96 * pv2$se.fit),
    upperCI = inverseFunction(pv2$fit + 1.96 * pv2$se.fit)
  )
crimeScene2
```

Here the probability of being male is close to 0.5, so the tool is essentially guessing. A foot length of 249 mm sits almost exactly at the "tipping point" where males and females are equally likely (around 250 mm, roughly the midpoint between the average female and male foot lengths), so this print tells us very little about the culprit's sex. This is an important lesson: a prediction is only as useful as the certainty attached to it.

## Power analysis: questions in the chapter

These answers are approximate: because the simulations are random, your numbers will differ slightly.

1) **What sample size would give you 80% power?** About 26 per group. You can find this by increasing `sampleSize` until the power reaches 0.8:

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-power-q1}
set.seed(42)
sampleSize <- 26 # vary this until power > 0.8
result <- replicate(
  1000,
  t.test(
    rnorm(sampleSize, mean = 12, sd = 3),
    rnorm(sampleSize, mean = 14.4, sd = 3)
  )$p.value
)
mean(result < 0.05)
```

2) **What power would you have if the variation was larger (sd = 4)?** With 10 per group, the power falls from about 40% to about 24%. More noise makes the signal harder to detect.

3) **What power would you have if the difference was only 10%?** The treatment mean would then be 12 $\times$ 1.1 = 13.2 mm, and with 10 per group the power falls to about 13%. Small effects are much harder to detect.

## Snails on the move


Simulate a t-test-based analysis in R to figure out what sample size would result in 80% power.


```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-80}
set.seed(42)
sampleSize <- 40 # vary this until power > 0.8
result <- replicate(
  1000,
  t.test(
    rnorm(sampleSize, mean = 7.4, sd = 2.76),
    rnorm(sampleSize, mean = 7.4 * 1.25, sd = 2.76)
  )$p.value
)
sum(result < 0.05) / 1000
```

You should find that you need a sample size of about 40 per group.

## Mouse lemur strength

What difference in strength could you reliably detect (with power >80%) with these sample sizes?

```{r 6-1-00-AllSolutions-81}
set.seed(42)
diff <- 185 # Vary this to give a difference to 2nd group t-test
result <- replicate(
  1000,
  t.test(
    rnorm(25, mean = 600, sd = 145),
    rnorm(8, mean = 600 - diff, sd = 145)
  )$p.value
)
sum(result < 0.05) / 1000
```

You should find that you could detect a difference of about 185g or a mean for old animals of 415g which is 70% of the young animals i.e. a 30% reduction.
